intact in vivo environment possesses complex neurohormonal regulatory networks,
hemodynamic adaptations, and multi-organ crosstalk. In sham-operated healthy mice,
the heart may counterbalance the direct hypertrophic stimuli of asprosin by activating
intrinsic compensatory pathways—such as antioxidant and anti-apoptotic mechanisms,
or metabolic reprogramming involving other organs—thereby maintaining myocardial
structural and functional homeostasis. Secondly, cellular heterogeneity and
microenvironment: In vitro models typically use purified cardiomyocyte cultures,
whereas the in vivo heart consists of multiple interacting cell types, including
cardiomyocytes, fibroblasts, endothelial cells, and immune cells. This integrated
microenvironment may secrete factors that antagonize asprosin’s actions or modulate
its bioactivity.
(2) The representative graphs of Fig 1M and Fig 2D did not show that the heart
LVPWd/s in TAC-AAV9-NC and TAC-AAV9-Asprosin groups was further thickened
compared with the corresponding control group.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment concerning the
representative images in Figures 1M and 2D, which highlight the observation that the
apparent increase in left ventricular posterior wall thickness during diastole (LVPWd)
in the TAC+AAV9-NC and TAC+AAV9-Asprosin groups, as compared to the control
groups, is not clearly discernible. We agree that this is an appropriate observation, and
we acknowledge that clearly discernible intergroup differences are essential for the
accurate interpretation of these experimental results. In response to the reviewer’s
suggestion, we have replaced the more representative echocardiographic images
showing left ventricular posterior wall thickness at diastole (LVPWd) in Figures 1M
and 2D in the revised manuscript. The updated figures clearly demonstrated that under
TAC-induced hypertrophic conditions, LVPWd is further increased in the TAC+AAV9-
Asprosin group compared to the TAC+AAV9-NC group (Figure R2A) (page9-10, line
173-177). Conversely, the TAC+AAV9-shFBN1 group showed a reduction in
4 / 37
ventricular wall thickness and improved ventricular function relative to the
TAC+AAV9-shNC group (Figure R2B) (page12, line 229-231). These updated images
provide direct visual evidence supporting our conclusion that AAV9-mediated
cardiomyocyte-specific asprosin overexpression exacerbates pressure overload-
induced cardiac hypertrophy, while cardiomyocyte-specific asprosin knockdown
attenuates this pathological remodeling. The aforementioned data have been
integrated into the revised manuscript (Figure 1M and Figure 2D).
Figure R2. Representative left ventricular ultrasound images (echocardiograms) of male mice hearts are
shown.
(3) It is recommended to verify glycolysis rates at the in vivo level, including fig3 and
fig6, and not only at the in vitro level.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable comments and thorough review of
our manuscript. The suggestion to validate glycolytic rate in vivo (in relation to Figures
3 and 6), is both critical and highly valuable. We fully agree that direct measurement of
glycolytic flux in a robust in vivo model is essential for translating our cellular findings
into broader physiological and pathological contexts.
As suggested, we isolated cardiomyocytes from in vivo models and conducted
Seahorse XF metabolic assays to further examine the role of the asprosin–PFKP axis in
regulating cardiomyocyte glycolytic metabolism. Extracellular acidification rate
(ECAR) measurements revealed a significant increase in glycolytic capacity in the
TAC+AAV9-Asprosin group compared to the TAC+AAV9-NC group (Figure R3A)
(page14, line 267–272). We also assessed the effects of cardiomyocyte-specific
asprosin overexpression on mitochondrial respiration in TAC-induced hypertrophic
5 / 37
cardiomyocytes. Oxygen consumption rate (OCR) analysis indicated that asprosin
overexpression markedly suppressed mitochondrial respiratory function, as shown by
reduced basal respiration, maximal respiration, spare respiratory capacity, and ATP
production-linked oxygen consumption (Figure R3B) (page14, line 267–272). The
aforementioned data have been integrated into the revised manuscript (Figure
S7C-D). These additional data provide in vivo evidence that asprosin enhances
glycolytic metabolism while impairing mitochondrial respiration, thereby supporting
our central conclusion.
Figure R3. ECAR and OCR assays are conducted to investigate the glycolytic and respiratory ability of adult
mice cardiomyocytes.
(A-B) ECAR (n=3) and OCR (n=6) of the cardiomyocytes isolated from adult mice were detected by seahorse in
the indicated groups. Statistical tests were performed using the unpaired two-tailed t-test in (A, B). **, P <0.01. ***, P
<0.001.
In parallel, we further assessed glycolytic flux and mitochondrial respiratory
function in vivo in the experimental groups associated with Figure 6 using Seahorse
XF technology. Results demonstrated that cardiomyocyte-specific knockdown of
asprosin significantly attenuated the TAC-induced elevation in both glycolytic capacity
and mitochondrial respiratory dysfunction (Figure R4A–B; page23, line 475–479).
Importantly, concomitant overexpression of PFKP largely reversed these protective
effects (Figure R4A–B; page23, line 475–479). These results further reinforce our
conclusion that asprosin promotes pathological cardiac hypertrophy through PFKP-
6 / 37
mediated enhancement of glycolytic metabolism. The aforementioned data have
been integrated into the revised manuscript (Figure S17A-B).
Figure R4. ECAR and OCR assays are conducted to investigate the glycolytic and respiratory ability of adult
mice cardiomyocytes.
(A-B) ECAR (n=3-4) and OCR (n=5) of the cardiomyocytes isolated from adult mice were detected by seahorse in
the indicated groups. Statistical tests were performed using the one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni's multiple
comparisons test in (A, B). *, P <0.05. **, P <0.01. ***, P <0.001.
(4) The manuscript involves the assay of OCR, and it is suggested that statistics of ATP
production are more convincing.
Response: We thank the reviewer for their insightful suggestions. As recommended,
we have reanalyzed the existing data and conducted additional experiments to more
rigorously evaluate the ATP production derived from our OCR measurements. The
results indicated that overexpression of either asprosin or PFKP led to a significant
reduction in ATP production capacity in NMCMs (Figures R5A, B) (page 14, line 274–
276 & page20, line 402–403). Furthermore, under angiotensin II (Ang II)-induced
hypertrophic conditions, asprosin overexpression markedly exacerbated the impairment
of ATP production (Figure R5C) (page14, line 272–274). In the rescue experiments,
knockdown of asprosin significantly ameliorated the Ang II-induced mitochondrial
dysfunction and concomitant decline in ATP generation. This protective effect was,
however, effectively abolished by concomitant PFKP overexpression (Figure R5D)
(page24, line 484–487). Moreover, treatment with dichloroacetate (DCA) significantly
reversed the PFKP overexpression-induced suppression of both mitochondrial
respiratory capacity and ATP production in NMCMs (Figure R5E) (page22, line 447–
450). Together, these data provide functional evidence that the asprosin–PFKP axis
7 / 37
impairs mitochondrial ATP generation, thereby contributing to pathological remodeling.
The aforementioned data have been integrated into the revised manuscript (Figure
S3H, Figure S13H, Figure 3H, Figure S17D, and Figure S13W).
Figure R5. OCR assays are conducted to investigate the NMCMs respiratory ability.
(A) OCR assay was performed to assess the impact of asprosin overexpression on the respiratory capacity of
NMCMs (n=3). (B) OCR assay was performed to assess the impact of PFKP overexpression on the respiratory
capacity of NMCMs (n=3-4). (C) Analysis and quantification of OCR (n=5) of the NMCMs in the indicated groups.
(D) Analysis and quantification of OCR (n=3) of the NMCMs in the indicated groups. (E) Analysis and quantification
of OCR (n=5) of the NMCMs in the indicated groups. Statistical tests were performed using the unpaired two-tailed
t-test in (A, B, C), and the one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni's multiple comparisons test in (D, E). *, P <0.05. **,
P <0.01. ***, P <0.001.
Importantly, we also quantitatively assessed intracellular ATP levels across all
experimental groups using a commercial ATP detection kit. Results showed that
8 / 37
physiological overexpression of either asprosin or PFKP was sufficient to reduce ATP
content in NMCMs (Figures R6A, B) (page14, line 276–278 & page20, 402–406).
Conversely, targeted knockdown of asprosin or PFKP significantly attenuated the Ang
II–induced reduction in ATP content of NMCMs (Figures R6C, D) (page14, line 282–
283 & page20, line 414–415). Furthermore, in vitro rescue experiments confirmed that
asprosin knockdown alleviated the Ang II–induced deficit in ATP supply, an effect that
was reversed by concomitant PFKP overexpression (Figure R6E) (page24, line 490–
491). The aforementioned data have been integrated into the revised manuscript
(Figure S3G, Figure S13I, Figure S6F, Figure S14I, and Figure S16I).
Figure R6. Analysis of the regulatory role of the asprosin-PFKP axis in modulating ATP content in NMCMs.
(A-E) The ATP contents in NMCMs was quantified using an ATP content assay kit (A, B, D: n=5; C: n=7; E: n=6).
Statistical tests were performed using the unpaired two-tailed t-test in (A, B), and the one-way ANOVA with
Bonferroni's multiple comparisons test in (C, D, E). *, P <0.05; ***, P <0.001.
(5) Table S3 lists Cpt1b, which is much more abundant than PFKP. Why not choose
Cpt1b? Does Asprosin have an effect on fatty acid oxidation?
Response: Thank you for your valuable comment. We fully agree that selecting a
protein with high expression is important; however, target selection must also consider
its biological relevance. First, accumulating evidence has demonstrated that asprosin
plays a critical role in regulating glucose metabolism homeostasis (PMID: 27087445,
31230984, 37769508, 36056803). Second, other studies have also confirmed that
asprosin significantly contributes to the regulation of fatty acid oxidation (FAO),
including modulating inflammatory responses via the AMPK signaling pathway, which
promotes the progression of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) (PMID:
37647445). However, KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of differentially expressed
9 / 37
genes from myocardial tissue RNA-seq in this study showed that the major pathways
influenced by asprosin were predominantly enriched in metabolic processes,
particularly those involved in glucose metabolism, central carbon metabolism in cancer,
pyruvate metabolism, and various amino acid metabolic pathways. In contrast, no
significant enrichment was observed in FAO-related pathways. This finding suggests
that asprosin may primarily regulate glucose metabolism in the context of pathological
cardiac hypertrophy. More importantly, ECAR experiments demonstrated that asprosin
overexpression enhanced glycolytic metabolism of NMCMs in this study.
PFKP, a key platelet isoform of phosphofructokinase (PFK1), is closely associated
with critical biological processes such as glycolytic metabolic shifts, energy
metabolism reprogramming, and downstream molecular mechanisms linked to
cardiovascular disease progression (PMID: 39419453). Importantly, existing literature
has established the regulatory roles of the liver-type (PFKL) and muscle-type (PFKM)
isoforms of phosphofructokinase in cardiovascular diseases (PMID: 36810848,
40222696, 40569576, 35450439), further supporting the involvement of PFKP in
pathological cardiac hypertrophy. More importantly, the latest study has further
highlighted the critical role of PFKP in the regulation of pathological cardiac
hypertrophy (PMID: 39419453). In contrast, CPT1B primarily participates in FAO and
exhibits a relatively weak association with the core metabolic phenotypes observed in
our study. Therefore, the selection of PFKP—over CPT1B—as the downstream target
of asprosin is supported by the aforementioned evidence, as it not only aligns with its
well-established function in glucose homeostasis but also offers greater mechanistic
relevance and scientific merit.
In response to the reviewer’s suggestion, we performed additional experiments
involving asprosin overexpression in cardiomyocytes to evaluate its effects on key
markers of FAO. qRT-PCR analysis revealed that asprosin overexpression led to a
modest decrease in the mRNA expression of several critical FAO-related genes,
including CPT1B, LCAD, PGC-1α, ACOX1, and PPARα (Figure R7A). However,
these changes did not reach statistical significance. Importantly, western blot analysis
10 / 37
further confirmed that asprosin overexpression did not significantly alter CPT1B
protein expression (Figure R7B).
Figure R7. Asprosin does not exert a significant regulatory effect on FAO-related genes in NMCMs.
(A) qRT-PCR was performed to detect the FAO-related genes mRNA expression levels (CPT1B: n=5; LCAD,
PPARα, PGC1α, ACOX1: n=6). (B) Western blot was performed to detect CPT1B protein expression levels (n=6).
Statistical tests were performed using the unpaired two-tailed t-test in (A, B). ns, not significant.
We sincerely appreciate your insightful question. Dysregulation of FAO represents
a hallmark of metabolic remodeling in heart failure (PMID：28192373). Although our
data do not support a significant role for asprosin in the transcriptional regulation of
FAO genes, further investigations at the functional level may yield valuable insights
into its potential involvement in FAO. We are deeply grateful for your valuable
comments on our manuscript. Your thoughtful suggestions will contribute to a more
comprehensive understanding of the specific mechanisms by which asprosin modulates
FAO in cardiac diseases and provide meaningful references for the development of
potential cardiovascular therapeutic targets.
(6) Methods for isolating CMs, CFs, SMC and EC from adult mouse hearts and
identification of cell types are lacking.
Response: We are grateful for your valuable comments. Your meticulous attention to
methodological details has encouraged us to provide a clearer and more thorough
explanation regarding the experimental approach. We would like to clarify that the cells
utilized in Figure 1J consisted of neonatal mouse-derived primary cardiomyocytes
11 / 37
(NMCMs), neonatal mouse-derived primary cardiac fibroblasts (NMCFs), as well as
mouse aortic smooth muscle cell lines (SMCs) and mouse aortic endothelial cell lines
(ECs). The aim of this experiment was to efficiently evaluate the effect of Ang II on
asprosin expression across various cardiac cell types. The use of neonatal mouse
primary cells is a well-established approach in cardiovascular research, owing to their
higher viability and enhanced proliferative capacity in vitro, which makes them
particularly suitable for phenotypic assays. We recognize that the original description
in the Methods and Results sections may not have sufficiently emphasized the
distinction between cell sources, which could have led to misunderstanding. We
sincerely apologize for this lack of clarity. In the revised version of the manuscript,
we will ensure that the origin of the cells used in Figure 1J is explicitly stated to prevent
any potential ambiguity and to improve the overall precision and readability of the study.
We fully concur with your perspective on the importance of using adult mouse
cardiac cells to validate the physiological relevance of our findings. Indeed, this
approach constitutes a central element of our experimental design. As described in later
sections of the manuscript, adult mouse cardiomyocytes were isolated using the
established langendorff perfusion technique (PMID: 23861485, 27502479), and
carefully characterized through immunofluorescence staining—including confirmation
with anti-α-actinin antibody (Figure R8A). These rigorously validated cells provided
the essential foundation for subsequent functional analyses, such as Seahorse metabolic
assays. Data obtained from experiments utilizing adult cardiomyocytes are consistent
with and strongly support the NMCMs results, together reinforcing the main
conclusions of this study. The aforementioned data have been integrated into the
revised manuscript (Figure S2B).
12 / 37
Figure R8. (A) Representative immunofluorescence images showing α-actinin staining for the identification
of isolated adult mouse cardiomyocytes. Red: α-actinin; Blue: DAPI; Light：Light cells
(7) The discussion section should also focus on the current research status of the role
of Asprosin in the heart, including ischemic cardiomyopathy, diabetic cardiomyopathy,
etc., and whether its mechanism of action is relevant to this study?
Response: Thanks for reviewer`s invaluable advice. We sincerely appreciate your
meticulous review and insightful comments on our manuscript. Your suggestion that
"the discussion section should further focus on the mechanism of asprosin in heart
diseases (ischemic cardiomyopathy and diabetic cardiomyopathy) and its relevance to
the findings of this study" is highly constructive. In response to your recommendation,
we have incorporated the following additions and in-depth discussions in the revised
manuscript (page 27-28, line 552-578).
(8) While DTX3L is identified as the E3 ligase for PFKP, other ubiquitin-modifying
enzymes (e.g., deubiquitinases) may contribute.
Response: Thanks for reviewer`s invaluable advice. Indeed, multiple studies have
reported PFKP ubiquitination by different regulators, such as USP5, Trim21, HRD1,
and RNF123, in various pathological contexts (PMIDs: 38217030, 39308018,
33588886, 39725718). In this study, we employed Co-IP coupled with mass
spectrometry (MS) to identify E3 ligases interacting with PFKP in NMCMs. As shown
in Table S3, enzymes including USP5, Trim21, HRD1, and RNF123 were not
significantly enriched in the PFKP immunoprecipitation complex. This may be
attributed to weak or transient interactions between these enzymes and PFKP, or their
13 / 37
low basal expression levels in NMCMs. Significantly, our functional experiments
provided robust evidence for the DTX3L–PFKP interaction; DTX3L overexpression
enhanced PFKP ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation, whereas the catalytically
inactive DTX3L mutant failed to regulate PFKP ubiquitination. Collectively, these
findings establish DTX3L as a key E3 ubiquitin ligase involved in the regulation of
PFKP stability.
We sincerely appreciate your insightful comments on the regulatory mechanisms
of ubiquitination. The perspective you highlighted — that "other ubiquitination-
modifying enzymes, such as deubiquitinating enzymes or yet-to-be-characterized E3
ligases, may also participate in the regulation of PFKP" — is highly valuable. We
completely concur that the ubiquitination process is inherently complex and typically
involves the coordinated interplay of multiple enzymatic components. This study is
primarily aimed at identifying the core E3 ligase responsible for mediating PFKP
degradation in NMCMs. However, we also recognize that the ubiquitination status of
PFKP may be dynamically regulated by additional factors, such as both well-
characterized and yet-to-be-identified E3 ubiquitin ligases. Importantly, we have
incorporated in-depth discussions in the revised manuscript (page30, line 627-629).
Reviewer #2: (Remarks to the Author):
Ming Tong et al. found that plasma asprosin levels were significantly higher in patients
with hypertensive heart failure than in non-heart failure patients. These findings align
with previous studies showing that serum asprosin levels are elevated in heart failure
patients, including those with hypertensive heart failure (PMID: 38097977IF: 2.3 Q2),
as well as in patients with coronary artery disease (PMID: 34419063IF: 4.2 Q1) and
dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) (PMID: 32894050IF: 2.3 Q2). However, I am surprised
that the authors neither discussed nor referenced any existing literature associating this
adipokine with cardiovascular disease in their manuscript. The novelty of this study lies
in the authors' demonstration that overexpressing asprosin induces pathological
hypertrophy, while transgenic mice with reduced asprosin expression are protected
against TAC-induced hypertrophy. They also observed that an inhibitor, BOS-318,
reversed hypertrophy in a cell model. However, despite conducting multiple in vivo
experiments, they have not yet tested the therapeutic potential of this inhibitor in a TAC
model, which would be a critical step in evaluating its translational relevance for heart
failure treatment.
The authors propose that asprosin binds to and inhibits the ubiquitination-mediated
degradation of phosphofructokinase platelet (PFKP). Consistent with a study published
14 / 37
earlier this year (Biochimica et Biophysica Acta - Molecular Basis of Disease, DOI:
10.1016/j.bbadis.2024.167542), they demonstrate that cardiac-specific knockout of
PFKP alleviates cardiac hypertrophy.
Major concerns:

reversed by concomitant overexpression of PFKP. (Figure R18E, F) (page24, line 495-

upregulates PDK4 and inhibits PDH activity, thereby impairing the conversion of
pyruvate to acetyl-CoA. This results in pyruvate accumulation and reduced acetyl-CoA
levels, providing a direct mechanistic explanation for the observed suppression of
mitochondrial respiration, elevated lactate production, and alterations in ΔΨm. Your

our study, and we are grateful for your guidance in strengthening this work. The
aforementioned data have been integrated into the revised manuscript (Figure

production or enhanced TCA cycle flux)—is crucial for further refining the metabolic
mechanisms underlying our findings. In this study, our previous experimental results
have demonstrated that PFKP plays a pivotal role in pathological cardiac hypertrophy
by modulating the PDK4/PDH axis (Figure R16A-F and Figure R17A-D). Besides,
we demonstrated that the mechanism underlying the benefits of PFKP knockdown lies
in its capacity to reduce Ang II-induced PDH phosphorylation, leading to enhanced
PDH activity, increased TCA cycle flux, and improved mitochondrial function, as

opposed to a mechanism involving LDHA-directed pyruvate-to-lactate conversion. We
highly value your suggestions. Building upon these insights, we plan to incorporate
more comprehensive detection and analysis of LDHA in future studies to further
elucidate the role of the asprosin-PFKP axis in regulating cardiovascular diseases
through lactate production. This line of investigation will not only expand the current
understanding of this research field but also provide novel perspectives into the
metabolic regulatory network in cardiovascular pathophysiology.

oxidative metabolism, and thereby reduces Δψm and promotes hypertrophy. If so,
inhibiting PDK or LDHA would promote TCA flux and oxidative metabolism,
potentially alleviating hypertrophy. Conversely, PDH inhibition might worsen
pathology. Pharmacological modulation of the PDK–PDH axis would help clarify the

instrumental in enhancing the mechanistic and translational depth of our study. In
response, we performed additional experiments using the PDK inhibitor DCA. NMCMs
were divided into the following groups: 1) empty vector control (Vector), 2) asprosin
overexpression (Asprosin), and 3) asprosin overexpression with DCA treatment
(Asprosin+DCA). Western blot and qPCR analyses revealed that DCA treatment
significantly attenuated asprosin-induced cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, as indicated by
reduced expression of hypertrophy markers (ANP, BNP, and β-MHC) and decreased

(Figure R19D–G) (page24, line 500-504). These findings demonstrate that
pharmacological inhibition of PDK by DCA corrects the metabolic reprogramming
induced by the asprosin–PFKP axis and mitigates subsequent pathological hypertrophy.

pathway but also underscore its potential as a therapeutic target. The aforementioned
data have been integrated into the revised manuscript (Figure S18E-K).

suggestion to investigate the connection between the FBN1 (asprosin)-PFKP axis and
classical cardiac hypertrophy signaling pathways is highly valuable, as it will
significantly deepen our understanding of the crosstalk between metabolic
reprogramming and signal transduction. We concur with your perspective and wish to
highlight that accumulating evidence indicates both asprosin and PFKP independently
contribute to the activation of the ERK1/2 signaling pathway (PMID: 38677690,

31194992, 38982480). Based on this knowledge, we have further explored whether the
asprosin-PFKP axis contributes to the pathogenesis of pathological cardiac hypertrophy
through modulation of the ERK1/2 signaling pathway. Our experimental results clearly
demonstrated (Figure R20A): in the Ang II-induced NMCMs pathological cardiac
hypertrophy model, the ERK1/2 pathway was significantly activated. However,
knockdown of FBN1 (which leads to asprosin deficiency) markedly suppressed the

node of the asprosin-PFKP axis.

context, the specific ERK1/2 inhibitor ulixertinib was administered concurrently in the

study not only confirms the presence of the asprosin-PFKP axis in the context of cardiac

classical ERK1/2 signaling pathway, thereby providing initial mechanistic insights into
how metabolic regulators interface with core signaling cascades.
However, we also recognize that other classical signaling pathways—such as those
mediated by NFAT, Akt, and mTOR—may interplay with asprosin in regulating
pathological cardiac hypertrophy, which represents an important direction for future
research. We greatly appreciate your valuable insights, which have significantly

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: The author have addressed most of the concerns of the reviewers', and the manuscript is now acceptable.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
I appreciate the authors’ extensive dataset and the scope of experimentation, and I thank them for addressing many of my
prior comments. Their clarifications were helpful and several suggestions appear to have been incorporated. That said, two
substantive concern remains unresolved.
The reported ejection fraction for the same control condition (TAC + AAV9-NC) differs markedly between Figures 1.O and
2.F (≈40% vs ≈55%). If these panels are meant to represent the same control condition, such a discrepancy would likely be
statistically significant under an appropriate test. While variability is expected in vivo, the pattern here is troubling: the control
EF appears to move opposite to the experimental group (higher when the experimental EF is lower, and vice versa) and
could raise concerns about analysis bias.
It remains unclear whether the immunoprecipitation (IP) in Figure 4B worked as intended and I remain concerned about the
validity of the co-IP. In a well-performing IP, especially a FLAG-IP designed for purification, the Flag-protein should be
enriched in the IP fraction relative to the input. However, the uncropped blot (R9A) shows asprosin markedly reduced versus
input, while the PFKP co-IP band appears stronger than Flag-asprosin, a pattern more consistent with inefficient pull-down or
non-specific carry-over (e.g., inadequate wash stringency). To resolve this, please provide full uncropped blots for Figure
4B with molecular-weight markers and matched exposures and include essential controls: anti-FLAG beads incubated with
lysate lacking FLAG-asprosin (negative control) ± His-tagged PFKP and beads-only control. A total-protein stain (Ponceau
or Coomassie) to document loading would further strengthen the evidence. Without such controls and clear enrichment of
asprosin, it is difficult to conclude that the IP was successful or that the PFKP co-IP reflects a specific interaction rather than
artefact.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
The authors have provided a detailed and constructive rebuttal, together with substantial new experimental data. I greatly
appreciate their sincere efforts to address my previous concerns in a thorough and transparent manner.
Key findings:
This study convincingly demonstrates that asprosin stabilizes PFKP and induces metabolic remodeling in pathological
cardiac hypertrophy via the PDK4–PDH pathway. Of particular importance, the authors provide compelling in vivo and in
vitro evidence that FBN1-derived asprosin acts specifically in cardiomyocytes and contributes to the mechanisms underlying
cardiac hypertrophy. These findings add both novelty and persuasiveness to the field.
Significance and originality:
The study goes beyond the established concept of asprosin as an adipose-derived adipokine and instead introduces the
novel idea that cardiomyocyte-derived asprosin directly contributes to metabolic remodeling and pathological hypertrophy.
The significance and originality of this concept are clearly demonstrated.
Support for conclusions:
The additional experiments—including PFKP knockdown and overexpression, FBN1 mutant analysis, and pharmacological
inhibition with a Furin inhibitor—strongly support the asprosin dependency of the observed effects. While rescue
experiments with exogenous asprosin in the shFBN1 knockdown model were not performed, the current evidence is
sufficient to support the conclusions.
Data analysis and interpretation:
No major issues are identified. The asprosin–PFKP interaction is supported by new pulldown data; however, the evidence is
not sufficient to definitively conclude “direct binding.” More cautious terminology such as “interaction” or “binding” would
therefore be more appropriate.
Methodological rigor:
The overall methodology is sound and consistent with standards in the field. The rationale for IP-MS screening is well
justified by the biological background, the absence of interactions with candidate membrane proteins, and references to
previous studies reporting secreted proteins interacting with intracellular molecules. In addition, the roles of DTX3L under
basal conditions, isoform specificity among PFK family members, the PDK–PDH axis, and classical hypertrophic signaling
pathways have all been carefully examined, providing strong support for the conclusions.
Reproducibility and clarity:
The methods are described in sufficient detail in the Supplemental Information to ensure reproducibility. The reorganization
of Figures 3, 4, and 6 has improved clarity, and typographical errors have been appropriately corrected.
Overall assessment:
In conclusion, the authors’ responses are both sufficient and appropriate, convincingly addressing the major concerns raised in the previous round.
Although some questions remain for future investigation, the current revision provides robust evidence and offers clear value
for publication. I recommend acceptance after minor editorial revisions.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Responses to Reviewers’ Comments
Corresponding Author: Professor Yan Zhang
Dear Reviewers:
Thank you for your thoughtful letter and constructive advice. We sincerely appreciate
the comments provided by you and the reviewers regarding our manuscript
(NCOMMS-25-14208A) entitled “YY1/Asprosin/PFKP Axis Regulates Glycolytic
Metabolism and Exacerbates Pathological Cardiac Hypertrophy.”
We have carefully considered all the feedback and have made revisions accordingly. In
addition, we performed several new experiments as suggested, which further strengthen
our conclusions.
Below, we provide detailed, point-by-point responses to all reviewer comments.
Point-by-point Responses to The Reviewer’s Criticisms
Reviewer #1: (Remarks to the Author):
The author have addressed most of the concerns of the reviewers', and the manuscript
is now acceptable.
Response: We are thrilled to receive the reviewer's positive evaluation. Their guidance
throughout the review process has been instrumental in strengthening our manuscript,
and we are grateful for their time and expertise.
Reviewer #2: (Remarks to the Author):
I appreciate the authors’ extensive dataset and the scope of experimentation, and I thank
them for addressing many of my prior comments. Their clarifications were helpful and
several suggestions appear to have been incorporated. That said, two substantive
concern remains unresolved.
Major concerns:
1 / 9
(1) The reported ejection fraction for the same control condition (TAC + AAV9-NC)
differs markedly between Figures 1.O and 2.F (≈40% vs ≈55%). If these panels are
meant to represent the same control condition, such a discrepancy would likely be
statistically significant under an appropriate test. While variability is expected in vivo,
the pattern here is troubling: the control EF appears to move opposite to the
experimental group (higher when the experimental EF is lower, and vice versa) and
could raise concerns about analysis bias.
Response:
We sincerely appreciate your meticulous review of our data and your insightful
comments regarding the variation in ejection fraction values for the control group
between Figures 1.O and 2.F. We fully understand the concerns this discrepancy may
raise, particularly regarding analytical consistency and data interpretation. To ensure
the absolute reliability of our data, upon receiving the first round of reviewers'
comments, we promptly conducted a new and independent repeat experiment for the
entire set of experimental groups (Sham+AAV9-NC; TAC+AAV9-NC; TAC+AAV9-
Asprosin). This replication was designed to rigorously re-evaluate the regulatory role
and functional significance of cardiomyocyte-specific asprosin overexpression in TAC-
induced pathological hypertrophy.
The new experimental results showed that, compared with the Sham + AAV9-NC
group (mean EF: 78%), the model control group (TAC + AAV9-NC) exhibited a mean
EF of 42.6%, while the experimental group (TAC + AAV9-Asprosin) showed a further
reduced mean EF of 27.9% (Figure R1A-B). These findings consistently reaffirm the
regulatory role of cardiomyocyte-specific asprosin overexpression in exacerbating
TAC-induced pathological cardiac hypertrophy. Importantly, the mean EF of the newly
generated model control group (TAC + AAV9-NC) closely aligns with the value
observed for the TAC + AAV-shNC group in Figure 2F (mean EF: 41.5%) and falls
within the same baseline range as other established model groups. This concordance
establishes a coherent and reliable internal control framework, thereby strengthening
the consistency and reproducibility of our experimental data.
Consistent with your earlier concerns, our in-depth investigation revealed that the
2 / 9
initial discrepancies in cardiac function measurements across control groups were
attributable to biological variability within a specific experimental batch, rather than
systematic analytical bias. To ensure data integrity and reliability, we have
comprehensively updated the statistical analyses and experimental results from the new
animal cohort in this group within the revised manuscript (Figure 1M&O). These new
findings provide a more reliable and solid foundation for our central conclusions.
Figure R1. Assessment of cardiac function in mice using echocardiography.
(A-B) Representative M-mode echocardiogram of mice and quantitative analysis of EF, FS, LVPWd, LVPWs,
LVIDd, and LVIDs in different groups of mice described in indicated groups (Sham+AAV9-NC: n=10; TAC+AAV9-
NC: n=12; TAC+AAV9-Asprosin: n=13). Statistical tests were performed using the one-way ANOVA with
Bonferroni's multiple comparisons test in (B). ***, P <0.001.
3 / 9
(2) It remains unclear whether the immunoprecipitation (IP) in Figure 4B worked as
intended and I remain concerned about the validity of the co-IP. In a well-performing
IP, especially a FLAG-IP designed for purification, the Flag-protein should be enriched
in the IP fraction relative to the input. However, the uncropped blot (R9A) shows
asprosin markedly reduced versus input, while the PFKP co-IP band appears stronger
than Flag-asprosin, a pattern more consistent with inefficient pull-down or non-specific
carry-over (e.g., inadequate wash stringency). To resolve this, please provide full
uncropped blots for Figure 4B with molecular-weight markers and matched exposures
and include essential controls: anti-FLAG beads incubated with lysate lacking FLAG-
asprosin (negative control) ± His-tagged PFKP and beads-only control. A total-protein
stain (Ponceau or Coomassie) to document loading would further strengthen the
evidence. Without such controls and clear enrichment of asprosin, it is difficult to
conclude that the IP was successful or that the PFKP co-IP reflects a specific interaction
rather than artefact.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer's insightful comment regarding the
immunoprecipitation data. This has prompted us to clarify that Figure 4B was intended
to show an endogenous interaction in cardiomyocytes and did not employ a Flag-tag
antibody Co-IP. We recognized that the specific issues raised regarding the Flag-IP
procedure rightly pertain to Figure 4D, where we overexpressed Flag-asprosin in HEK-
293T cells. Below, we provided a comprehensive response to these pertinent concerns
about the experimental design and interpretation of the results in Figure 4D. We would
like to clarify that the western blot analysis was performed using the ODYSSEY dual-
channel infrared fluorescence detection system, and the images were acquired and
processed with Image Studio software. During the preparation of Figure 4D, the
display intensity of the FLAG-asprosin channel was appropriately reduced to clearly
visualize band morphology and prevent signal saturation. We acknowledge that the data
presentation may have obscured a clear interpretation of the immunoprecipitation
results, and we apologize for any valid questions it has raised regarding the reliability
of the apparently stronger PFKP signal compared to Flag-asprosin.
In this study, all co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) experiments investigating the
interaction between Flag-asprosin and HA-PFKP were performed using the Pierce™
Co-Immunoprecipitation Kit (Thermo Fisher, #26149), which effectively circumvented
the non-specific interference from co-eluting antibody heavy and light chains inherent
4 / 9
to traditional Protein A/G magnetic bead methods by covalently immobilizing
antibodies onto amine-reactive resins. As recommended, the following co-
immunoprecipitation experimental groups were included to further validate the binding
interaction between Flag-asprosin and HA-PFKP:
1) Experiment group lane: Immunoprecipitation (IP) was performed using anti-Flag
coupling resins on lysates co-expressing Flag-asprosin and HA-PFKP.
2) Antibody negative control lane: The same co-expression lysate was subjected to IP
using mouse IgG isotype control antibody coupled to resins.
3) Flag-tag specificity control lane: Lysates expressing HA-PFKP alone (without
Flag-asprosin) were immunoprecipitated with anti-Flag coupling resins to assess
binding specificity dependent on the Flag tag.
4) Coupling resins background control lane: HA-PFKP lysates were incubated with
coupling resins alone (no antibody) to evaluate non-specific adsorption to the resins.
5) Cellular background control lane: Lysates from cells transfected with empty
vector were used for IP with anti-Flag coupling resins to rule out non-specific
interactions mediated by overexpression or cellular components.
6) Absolute negative control lane: Pure RIPA lysis buffer was incubated with
antibody-free conjugated resins to confirm absence of contamination or signal from
resins.
For western blot analysis, the entire Co-IP eluate was loaded, while the input
control represented 1% of the total cell lysate volume. The results are shown in Figure
R2A. Based on the complete uncropped blots (Figure R2A), the following conclusions
can be drawn: 1) Specific Enrichment and Interaction: In the experiment group lane
(Lane 1), anti-Flag coupling resins efficiently immunoprecipitated Flag-asprosin from
lysates co-expressing Flag-asprosin and HA-PFKP, with clear co-precipitation of HA-
PFKP. The markedly stronger signal of Flag-asprosin relative to HA-PFKP further
supports effective pull-down and a specific interaction. 2) Absence of Antibody-
5 / 9
Mediated Non-Specific Binding: No Flag-asprosin or HA-PFKP bands were detected
when anti-IgG coupling resins were used (Lane 2), indicating that the observed
interaction is not attributable to non-specific binding. 3) Dependency on Flag-asprosin
Expression: In all samples lacking Flag-asprosin expression (Lanes 3–6), HA-PFKP
was not pulled down, irrespective of whether anti-Flag (Lanes 3&5) or bare coupling
resins (Lanes 4&6) were used, demonstrating that the interaction strictly requires the
presence of Flag-asprosin.
We performed Coomassie Brilliant Blue staining on the eluted Co-IP samples as
suggested by the reviewer. As shown in Figure R2B (Lane 1), two specific protein
bands (with molecular weights below 35 kDa and approximately 100 kDa, respectively)
were clearly observed in the lysates co-expressing Flag-asprosin and HA-PFKP
following immunoprecipitation with anti-Flag conjugated resin. Crucially, the
molecular sizes of these bands correspond to the expected sizes of Flag-asprosin and
HA-PFKP, respectively. In contrast, no characteristic bands for HA-PFKP or Flag-
asprosin were detected at the corresponding positions in any of the control lanes
(Figure R2B, Lane 2-6). Collectively, these results strongly support that the interaction
between Flag-asprosin and HA-PFKP is highly specific and reproducible.
6 / 9
Figure R2. Representative CO-IP original Coomassie Brilliant Blue staining and western image.
To further substantiate the rigor of our study, we performed additional co-
immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) assays. As shown in the Figure R3A (now included as
Figure 4D in the revised manuscript), we observed efficient and specific co-
precipitation between HA-PFKP and Flag-asprosin. This result effectively excludes
non-specific binding as a major contributing factor. We believe these additional data
satisfactorily address the reviewer's legitimate concerns and provide compelling
evidence for a specific interaction between asprosin and PFKP.
Figure R3. Representative image demonstrating the interaction between Flag-asprosin and HA-PFKP.
Reviewer #4: (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have provided a detailed and constructive rebuttal, together with substantial
new experimental data. I greatly appreciate their sincere efforts to address my previous
concerns in a thorough and transparent manner.
Key findings:
This study convincingly demonstrates that asprosin stabilizes PFKP and induces
metabolic remodeling in pathological cardiac hypertrophy via the PDK4–PDH pathway.
Of particular importance, the authors provide compelling in vivo and in vitro evidence
that FBN1-derived asprosin acts specifically in cardiomyocytes and contributes to the

The study goes beyond the established concept of asprosin as an adipose-derived
